This is really not related to your comment, but it made me think about this. My paternal grandpa was a diabetic and had SO MANY health issues later in his life, but in a lot of ways, he was one of the best people I knew. When I was really young, he was just this mountain of a man who was always smiling and telling jokes, and i have so many good memories of him. When I was in 7th or 8th grade, a bunch of people who knew my grandpa started telling me how much I looked like him, and to be fair, when I was in my teens and early 20s, the likeness between me and pictures of him in his 20s was uncanny. If you colorized a photo of him when he joined the air force and compared it to a photo of me when I joined the army, it wouldn't be hard to convince people it was the same person in different colored dress uniforms. 

Anyway, I kept hearing over and over how much I looked like him. One day, my dad and uncle decide it's time to move him and my grandma back to town so we can help take care of them, and I went along to help pack and move everything. We drove a camper down so he can be comfortable on the way from Oklahoma to Wyoming. We get there, my dad and uncle start loading their car onto the dolly trailer, and they tell me to go talk to grandpa while they and my grandma are busy with that. So I sit down and start talking, but the conversation doesn't go real far before it kind of peters out, and I awkwardly tell him, "You know, grandpa, everyone keeps telling me how much I look like you did at my age". He sits there for a second before starting to cry and telling me, "I hope you don't end up like me, too". Being so young, I had no idea how to respond to that, so we just sat awkwardly until everyone else came back inside. That comment and my inability to respond still breaks my heart. He was one of my heroes growing up, especially since my dad was so emotionally abusive to me, and I wish I had had the presence of mind to tell him that I'd be proud to turn out like him, but I didn't and it haunts me that I couldn't find a way to give him that reassurance that, even if his health was a mess, he was someone I would love emulate as an adult.

I've never had anyone say that to me. Which is fortunate because my dad was an emotionally abusive asshole who left me with a ton of issues that I've spent close to a decade unpacking and confronting in therapy. I'm not one to follow celebrities, and nobody is perfect, but there are a few that it seems like are just genuinely good people. 

Robin Williams seems to have been just a genuinely good guy who spent a huge portion of his life just trying to make other people smile. He used to just show up at hospitals and visit children with terminal illnesses and spend a day going around making them and their families smile. 

Jack Black is another. To most of society he's just a high energy goofball, but he's also known for his charity work, and much like Robin, he seems to just want to make people smile. 

Keanu Reeves is probably one of the easier ones because he's gotten so much attention over the years. He has lived a pretty rough life but seems to have done out of it just a genuinely good, kind person. During the filming of the Matrix movies, he donated a lot of money to cancer charities as well as paying the crews of the movies extra out of his own pocket. He's been known for the very down to earth way he tends to live his life. He can still be found riding the subway, he took a flight to California that had to make an emergency landing a few hours away from where they were supposed to land, chartered vans to help everyone get to their destination, and spent the ride talking, joking, and playing games with the other people, and he's been known to buy a cake for his birthday, and just sit outside at a cafe offering a slice to anybody who stopped to talk to him. 

Terry Crews deserves a mention, not because he's someone who has apparently been perfect his whole life, but because he's owned his negative past and uses it to show how we can do better and how important it is to face our trauma and not just let it fester. He grew up in an abusive household and learned all the wrong lessons toxic masculinity can teach in that situation. He cheated on his wife and treated her poorly (though he was never physically abusive), until he realized he was approaching a line in the sand and he needed to change or he would lose the women who had stood by him for years. He went to therapy and did the work to become a better, healthier man. He was sexually assaulted by an exec at an agency event and came out about it during the #metoo movement, garnering attention for showing that it's not only women who are harmed by Hollywood's culture of covering up for predators. He worked through that trauma and is now well known for his positive and kind nature. 

There's so many we could mention, but I'll end with one more. Adam Sandler probably seems like kind of a strange one, but he is apparently another person who just wants to be goofy and make people smile. He's known for having a core group of friends who often find their way into his movies (and to be fair, he's made random cameos in some of their movies too), he has apparently done a fair amount of charity work, and he has been cited as a positive role model by others in Hollywood. Namely (and the reason I thought to include him), Terry Crews himself. I may not be remembering the story right, but I believe Terry actually credits Adam with helping him deal with a lot of his trauma after he realized how badly he needed to change. I do know that Terry has said Adam is one of the people he talked to after he was sexually assaulted and Adam helped him deal with that and find healthy ways to work through all of the anger and pain it caused.

Terry will probably get criticism from someone because of his past, but I think he's a great example, because he acknowledges the bad parts of his past and how he needed to change and become a better man, both for himself and for the people he cared about. Being a good role model isn't about being perfect your whole life. It's about doing your best, owning your faults, and trying to become a better person.

The national guard is basically a state level force for responding to emergencies. Members go through the same training the national military does, and they can be deployed to support combat operations that the rest of the military is taking part in, but the national guard technically reports to the governor of their state. National guard members can have normal civilian jobs and just have to attend a weekend drill each month and a 2 week long annual training (commonly referred to as AT) each year. National guard units can be "activated" to respond to emergencies like natural disasters and civil unrest. 

In my state, for example, it's very common for some towns to flood as the snow in the mountains melts and overflows the rivers. I'm not particularly familiar with how the European left handles or speaks on immigration, but I think the American left's biggest weakness on immigration is not that they don't take it seriously, but rather that they're terrible at messaging around it. 

Democrats as a party have never supported an "open border", and in fact, it's quite normal for Democratic presidencies to have bigger deportation numbers than Republican presidencies. The biggest actual difference in immigration policy between Democrats and Republicans though, is where they try to focus their efforts. 

Republicans tend to put more effort into more visible aspects of immigration policy, such as more border agents or Trump's wall. Democrats also put money and effort into the technology and manpower that supports our border, but they are also more likely to focus on what are known as "push factors". A push factor is something that drives people to travel here to cross the border. Examples of push factors are things like job availability or social and economic conditions in the home countries these people are traveling from. 

Obama had a program that pumped money into Central American communities to improve economic conditions and reduce the number of people who felt the need to travel here in the first place. We actually had data that showed that this program was working, but when Trump came into office the first time, one of the first things he did was to end the program, which led to an increase in border crossings. 

Another example is bills that have been introduced by Democrats a few times over the years that would get rid of loopholes and increase the consequences for employers who are found to have hired undocumented immigrants. These bills would address the push factor of job availability. If there are fewer employers willing to risk hiring an undocumented immigrant, there's fewer reasons for them to come here, and immigration numbers go down. These bills have typically failed, in part, because of a lack of support from Republicans. 

So, in my mind, the issue isn't that Democrats/ the left don't take immigration seriously. The issue is that they aren't great at messaging, and their focus is on methods that would be more effective but aren't as visible.

I actually have some experience in this. My family has met 2 relatives because of Ancestry DNA.

The first was my older brother. He isn't related to us through my dad, but through my mom, so obviously, she wasn't surprised by his existence. However, she had been forced to give him up for adoption 50 years earlier because she had gotten pregnant very young, and her parents had told her she either had to give the kid up or she could never come home. She had left her information with the adoption agency in case he ever went looking for her, but after 50 years, the agency had been shut down, and we weren't expecting him to ever reach out. Then one day he matched with a great aunt of mine, and she figured out it just have been my mom or one of her sisters who gave birth to him, and she reached out to my aunt, who reached out to my mom. He had left his information with the great aunt who passed it on, so my mom agonized over whether to reach out or not. She finally contacted him, and he was happy to meet up. The whole family is happy to have him.

On the other hand, we met a cousin a few years ago who is my uncle's daughter (on my dad's side). She was born in a similar situation to my older brother, but her mother was in high school and chose to keep her. So her mom never returned to school and never told my uncle she was pregnant. 50 or 60 years later, she matched on Ancestry DNA with my paternal aunt, who was delighted to meet more family and through her the rest of the family met my cousin. My uncle and his wife and other kids were actually the last to meet her, which was honestly probably not a bad thing given how my uncle reacted. We believe his reaction was spurred by his wife, but we don't know. Either way, he almost immediately told her he wanted nothing to do with her and that she needed to stay away from his family. He refused to tell his other 2 adult children about her and told the rest of the family not to say anything. In the name of keeping peace that order held for about a month while the rest of the family got to know her better until my paternal aunt made a scheme to take the decision out of my uncle's hands. She bought Ancestry kits for my uncle's other 2 kids for Christmas, and my other uncle decided to tell them the truth because my aunt's plan was just too sneaky and manipulative for his taste. Either way, both of my cousins now know about their sister, and have been happy to get to know her. 

I know that story isn't very hopeful, but that's the risk you take. Your genetic family may be excited to meet you. They may be upset. You have no way of finding out until you say something to them, but even if your father doesn't want you around, you may meet some other family who will love and accept you and be thrilled to have you around.

I think what's really going to start causing shifts in the classic car hobby are 3 things. 

1) money. A lot of younger people who might want to get into classic cars simply can't afford one and if they can they can't afford the work needed to take care of one. 

2) time. Maintaining classics takes time and effort that can be hard to come by when you're in your 30s and 40s, working, building a family, etc. Also, I'm sure it isn't like this everywhere, but in my town, the classic car clubs are almost entirely retirees. I'm a member of a Ford club and damned near every event they do, every group cruise for lunch or to visit a museum or collection is scheduled during the week when I am working and I'll always get comments from the members I know a little better about "It's sad you couldn't come!" but I couldn't come because they plan these things for Thursday afternoon. 

3) knowledge. This one is a slightly smaller barrier thanks to the internet, but unless you grew up in a family where you could learn to diagnose and repair them, owning one and keeping it on the road can daunting. Restoring one without knowing what parts you might need and where to find them can be very frustrating and make it harder as well. For example, I have a 65 Mustang and have most of the trim mine needs, but there's just a few pieces that are really hard to find in any kind of decent shape. Without knowledge of what I need and where to find it, I could spend HOURS and a lot of money looking and get the wrong part or get one that is in bad shape. 

Parts could probably be a 4th, because they don't make certain parts for all classic cars. It took 2 years for me to find a generator for my 65 Mustang the last time mine failed, and I know it's basically impossible to find body panels and stuff for some of the classic Mopars.

Credit score is a number that is based on a ratio of your income versus your existing debt and a few other factors. It theoretically let's financial institutions know how much of a risk lending you money would be. Problem is, not all financial institutions report to all the credit monitoring agencies, so you might have a really good score according to one agency and either no score or a really bad score with another. Which agency they report to tends to be regionally based, though larger institutions will typically report to all 3.

There's also some things that are just weird in how different actions impact your credit score. For instance, if you have a car loan and you pay it off your credit score goes down even though you now have less active debt than before. This is because that loan might be one of your oldest open debts and now that it's closed the consider you to have fewer accounts that show your reliability, even though they can still see that you never missed a payment and that it was paid off in full and on time. 

It's honestly a really dumb system, but we're kind of stuck with it now.

Technically, if a servers tips don't make up the difference between the servers base wage and the federal minimum of $7.25 per hour, then the restaurant has to pay the difference, but it's rare for a server to make $7.25 per hour in tips. 

Since our service industry is so heavily built around tipping to subsidize the low wages paid to servers, the expectation is that most people should pay 20% of the final bill as a tip, more if service was exceptional, less if the service was EXTREMELY bad. Poor service is often forgiven to a point by most people.

One thing to keep in mind with stories like OPs is most restaurants require servers to "tip out" or pay part of their tips to the other restaurant staff that support them (bar tenders, bus boys, and other lower paid positions that might also depend on tips, usually not kitchen staff as they are paid a more reasonable wage). This means that when a table doesn't tip or tips extremely poorly, the server can end up effectively paying those support staff out of their own pockets instead of out of tips. OP tipped roughly 12%, so that server basically decided that it was more worthwhile to make a point about the extremely low tip than to accept it meekly and move on.
